**The email code survives a dismiss (2026-11-09).**

- What happened: the owner saw on the iPhone that a tap outside the email sheet on the code step closed it and threw everything away, so the person had to type the address again and ask for a new code, and asked how the large companies build it. The cause was step 04's rule for the sheet, "closing resets everything": the scrim tap, the Android back key and a sign-in that worked all ran one `close()`, which reset the step, the address, the digits and the countdown. Clerk cancels nothing on a dismiss: its docs say an email code stays valid for 10 minutes (its own UI uses the same 30-second resend cooldown), so the reset threw away a code that still worked. The most common trigger is a reflex: people tap the dimmed area to put the keyboard away. The large apps put a code entry on a full page, where there is no "outside", or, where it is a sheet (Stripe Link, Shop Pay), let the sheet close as every sheet does and make the mistake free: reopening lands on the same code step. Recovery over prevention. The owner approved the recommendation as a whole.
- Decisions: (1) a dismiss (the scrim, the Android back key) only hides the sheet: the step, the address, the typed digits and the countdown stay, the countdown keeps running while hidden, and only the error line clears, because it belongs to the moment; (2) "Continue with email" reopens the sheet where it was, with no new button, no label change and no extra line on the Sign In screen; (3) the attempt is dropped only on purpose: "Use a different email", a sign-in that worked, and a tap on Apple or Google, because Clerk replaces the client's sign-in attempt with the provider's own, so the code could not be verified afterwards (the Sign In screen remounts the sheet through a `key` when a provider is tapped); (4) a stale code is the server's call, not a timer's: after the ten minutes Clerk answers `verification_expired`, which the sheet already shows as "That code has expired. Please request a new one." with Resend under it; (5) a request still running when the sheet is dismissed finishes and keeps its result: a verify that worked signs the person in, a failed one waits as the error line for the next opening (a dismiss no longer bumps the session counter; "Use a different email" and a finished sign-in still do). Not built, each with its reason in the recommendation: an inert scrim on the code step (it breaks what every phone user expects of a sheet and removes the scrim's "Close" for VoiceOver users), a confirmation dialog on the dismiss (a dialog over a sheet is the one-Modal-at-a-time case on iOS this app already works around), and a button label that changes while a code is pending. This supersedes step 04's "closing resets everything" for this sheet (Bottom Sheets).
- Changed: `src/screens/auth/EmailSheet.tsx` (`close()` became `dismiss()`, which clears the error line and calls `onClose`, and `finish()`, which resets everything after a sign-in that worked; the `BottomSheet` takes `dismiss`) and `src/screens/auth/SignInScreen.tsx` (`emailSheetKey`, bumped when a provider is tapped and passed as the sheet's `key`). No copy string, token, class name, package, server or migration changed, so a reload carries it in Expo Go and TestFlight needs a build.
- Verified (no phone): `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint` exit 0. No suite in `supabase/tests` loads the auth screens, so the proof is a scratch render check of the real `EmailSheet`, `BottomSheet`, `PrimaryButton` and `SignInScreen`, kept outside the repo (the repo's own TypeScript loader, a small fake React with hooks, effects and host refs, react-native faked as host names with a Modal that mounts its children only while visible, virtual timers, and a fake auth hook whose requests the check settles by hand): 10 of 10. A tap on the scrim keeps the code step with the address, three typed digits and a countdown that kept running while hidden (30, 27 before the dismiss, 22 on the reopen), asks for no second code, and the reopen focuses the code field; the Android back key behaves the same; the error line is the one thing a dismiss clears; "Use a different email" resets to the email step and keeps the typed address in the field, as before; a sign-in that worked resets everything; a code request and a verify still on their way when the sheet is dismissed finish and keep their result (the code step on reopen; a wrong code waiting as the error line with empty boxes, and no focus call while hidden); the countdown runs out while hidden and Resend works on reopen; on the real Sign In screen the same button reopens the code step with the same address and a tap on Google drops the attempt (the email button waits while Google runs and is back after a cancel, with nothing shown); and the sheet's chrome is unchanged (one scrim labelled Close, a transparent sliding Modal with the back key wired, its own safe-area provider). Thirteen deliberate breaks, served to the check in place of the repo files and never written to the repo, were each caught by a named check: the old reset on a dismiss; a dismiss that bumps the session, keeps the error line, zeroes the countdown, clears the digits, drops the address or goes back to the email step; a finished sign-in that keeps the step; the scrim wired to the reset; a wrong code that never shows its line; and on the Sign In screen no key bump, a key bumped but not passed, and a remount on every open. A first form of the tenth break was equivalent (a gate on `visible` inside the verify's stale closure) and was replaced. Two harness lessons: on Windows a `process.exit` right after `console.log` to a pipe drops the output (set `process.exitCode`), and an `act` helper must never await a handler's own promise (Send's handler awaits the request the check settles later, a deadlock).
- Not verified: the phone (the walk-through below), VoiceOver (the scrim's label and the sheet's controls are unchanged), Android, and how long Clerk keeps the attempt itself when the app stays open for hours (its docs give the code 10 minutes; a stale code shows the expired line with Resend).
- Known limits: the kept state lives in the mounted screen, so a force-quit starts fresh; a person who dismisses and comes back after ten minutes meets "That code has expired" and one Resend; the Sign In screen gives no cue that a code is pending (a decision, above).
- Phone walk-through: not run yet.

**The processing screen becomes a four-second handoff, and speech runs behind the answer (2026-11-09).**

- What happened: the owner sent a screenshot of New Entry's processing overlay (the pulsing mark, "Listening, praying, and finding scripture…", three step cards, a note, Close) and said it lasted about 30 seconds, which kills retention; they wanted at most 4 seconds, with no loss in the reflection's quality, built the way the large consumer apps build a step like this. Measured in the step 36 and 37 walk-throughs a reflection took 21 to 33 seconds end to end, of which the spoken devotional (Cloud Text-to-Speech and its upload) was 12 to 15 seconds and the model 5 to 10; the overlay waited the whole of it (`WAIT_MS` 90 s), and the quality lives in the model's reply and the voice, which the wait never improved.
- Decisions (the agent's recommendation, approved as a whole; none struck): (1) **Send and go.** New Entry waits `NEW_ENTRY_WAIT_MS` (4 s, the engine's `WAIT_MS`) and hands the reflection to Journal, where its card shows the progress and turns into the reflection; no quality knob changed (the prompt, the models, the voice and every check are as they were). (2) **Progressive delivery on the server.** `process-entry` answers as soon as the reflection and its affirmations are saved, and speech runs behind the answer in `EdgeRuntime.waitUntil` (Backend requirements 12 and 13), so the text reaches the phone 12 to 15 seconds earlier and the audio lands a few seconds after it. (3) **The overlay is a confirmation**, not a waiting room: the pulsing mark and "Saving your reflection…", then at `NEW_ENTRY_SAVED_AT_MS` (2.6 s) a sage check springs onto the mark's rim with "Saved" and "Your devotional is being prepared. It’ll be in your Journal in a moment."; nothing to press, and the Close button, the step cards and the note are gone; the failure view (the phone could not save, or the server refused) is unchanged. (4) **The Journal card shows the stages** New Entry used to show: a thin plum progress bar that moves to each stage the sync engine reports (receiving 22%, reflecting 58%, preparing 86%; `STAGE_TIMELINE` is 3 s and 9 s now, for the usual 10 to 30 seconds) and creeps within one so it never looks stuck, over the stage's line; under Reduce Motion it jumps. (5) **An audio-pending state** everywhere a reflection shows: `isAudioPending(entry, nowMs)` in `data/selectors.ts` (ready, a devotional, no audio path, no `TTS_FAILED`, changed within `AUDIO_PENDING_MS`, 2 minutes), the Journal card's "Preparing audio" chip, Reflection's player card "Preparing your audio. You can read the devotional below." (a polite live region), the hook's `audioPending`, and the hook's 5-second reads while Realtime is not live, as for an entry still being prepared (Realtime's `entry_changed` on the speech update is the usual way the audio arrives). (6) **The success tap moves to Journal** (the engine's `finished` event; never for a heavy moment): New Entry no longer sees the answer. (7) **`reflection_ready` loses `has_audio`**: it would always read false now. (8) **The Paywall is no longer opened by New Entry on the free limit** unless the 402 comes inside the 4 seconds: the limit's card with See plans does it, as it already did for a limit found later. (9) The developer check waits for the audio behind the answer (every 3 s, up to 60 s) and compares "same id again" by id, creation time and script, because the speech update moves `updated_at`. (10) No package, migration, secret, policy or `app.json` change; the hosted functions need a deploy of `process-entry` (development, then production, the owner's).

**The processing screen keeps its three steps and completes in three seconds (2026-11-10).**

- What happened: the owner sent a screenshot of the old processing screen (the pulsing mark, "Listening, praying, and finding scripture…", the three step cards, the note and Close, from TestFlight build 9) and said what they meant the day before: keep this screen, but the whole processing, about 30 seconds, should take about 3 seconds to complete, with no loss in the reflection's quality, built as Google, Facebook or Amazon would build it. The 2026-11-09 entry had replaced the screen with a check badge; this entry puts the three step cards back and makes the screen complete in three seconds.
- Where the 30 seconds go, measured in the step 36 and 37 walk-throughs and the tone evaluation (a written entry, `gemini-3.8-flash`): the crisis screening 2.7 to 2.8 s, the reflection 7 to 9 s (median 7.4 to 8.8) plus a retry on about a third of reflections (6 to 8 s more: the hook guard and the tone checks), the affirmation verses' follow-up 1 to 3 s when a verse breaks a rule, the Bible under 0.5 s, the database 0.5 to 2 s from Lagos (about 0.2 s from the US), and the spoken devotional 12 to 15 s. The speech already runs behind the answer since 2026-11-09, which is a cut of 12 to 15 s. The rest is the model's own time on the model the owner chose for quality: a real completion in three seconds is not possible without changing the model, so the three seconds are the screen's, and the server's work finishes in the Journal's card. The one server cut left that costs no quality is to screen a written entry and write its reflection in parallel (about 2.5 s; a heavy or failed screening discards the parallel reply), which changes the order of a crisis rule and waits for the owner's yes.
- Decisions (the agent's, on the owner's request; none asked again): (1) the screen is the owner's: the mark, the heading, the subtitle, the three step cards and the note; no Close button, because the screen leaves by itself in three seconds and a button that shows for three seconds invites a tap race. (2) A step card says Done only when its thing is done, so the cards name the phone's own moments: "Saving" becomes "Saved" once the reflection is in the outbox, "Sending" becomes "Sent" once the processor hands the request to the server, and "Preparing your devotional" is in progress when the screen leaves. The old labels "Listening" and "Reflecting" could not honestly say Done in three seconds (the model's work is 5 to 10 s). (3) Each tick waits for its moment on the screen as well as its fact (`NEW_ENTRY_STEP_SAVED_MS` 400 ms, `NEW_ENTRY_STEP_SENT_MS` 1.2 s), so a person sees the cards tick in turn and never all at once. (4) `NEW_ENTRY_WAIT_MS` is 3 s (the engine's `WAIT_MS`), and `NEW_ENTRY_SAVED_AT_MS` is gone. (5) The processor reports `receiving` when it hands the request to the server, after a recording's upload (before, at the start of the attempt): "Sent" is then true for a voice entry too, and the Journal card's bar starts from the request. (6) Everything else of 2026-11-09 stands: the server answers with the text and speaks behind it, the Journal card's bar and lines, the audio-pending state, the success tap on Journal, `reflection_ready` without `has_audio`, the Paywall from the card's See plans unless the 402 comes inside the 3 s. (7) Nothing installed, no migration, no secret, no server change.

They asked how a Christian team would build the prayer section. The recommendation (five moves, the despair rule, petitions tied to the devotional's next step, a longer prayer, a new rubric criterion and four new cases, compared with gen-v2.5 on the same model) was approved as written: "Implement recommend changing (gen-v2.6, the prayer only)".

**The active tab is its icon alone (2026-11-12).**

- What happened: the owner sent a screenshot of the tab bar with Scholar active (its filled icon over a plum "Scholar" label inside the lens) and asked that the active tab show only its icon, with no label, while the inactive tabs keep their icon and label; that the active icon be a little bigger than an inactive one; and that the growth be smooth, sleek and not too fast.
- Decisions (the owner's request; the values are the agent's, none asked again): (1) An inactive tab is as it was: its outline icon (22, `mauve`) over its label (`mauve` Medium). The active tab is its filled icon alone, 26 (18% larger), `plum`, in the middle of the tab, which is the middle of the lens; its label is not drawn. (2) One value per tab (0 inactive, 1 active) runs the whole change. The label is gone within the first 40% of the way, sinking 4 as it fades, which keeps it just ahead of the icon. The outline icon and the filled one cross-fade while they come down to the middle (half of what the label takes under the icon: 7.5 at normal text, following the system text size up to the label's 1.3 cap) and grow as one. Each icon is drawn at its own size (the outline one scaled up on its way out, the filled one scaled up from 22/26 on its way in), so both are sharp at rest. (3) The motion is a spring with no overshoot (`TAB_SPRING`: `stiffness` 160, `damping` 26, `mass` 1; critical damping is about 25.3): a soft start, half-way at about 0.13 s, nine tenths at about 0.31 s, landed at about 0.52 s, so the icon settles as the lens does. It replaces the 150 ms timed cross-fade and the growth of the whole icon-and-label block to 1.06 (`FADE_MS`, `ACTIVE_SCALE`). A spring and not a timed ease-out, because it starts from rest like the lens's own spring; no bounce, because the lens is the one thing in the bar that wobbles. (4) Unchanged: the lens (its pill shape, size, glass, spring and stretch), the capsule, the dock, the press feedback (0.6 and 0.96), the `selection` tick, the `tabPress` contract and the spoken labels: the Pressable still names every tab ("Scholar, tab, 2 of 4"), so a screen reader hears the active tab's name although it is not drawn. (5) Under Reduce Motion the label and the icon switch at once. (6) The bar no longer draws the active screen's name, and since 2026-10-31 the header draws only the wordmark, so each tab's own first lines carry it (the Journal's greeting, "Ask Scholar", "Sanctuary Prayers", Profile's account header). (7) Nothing installed; no new class name, token, theme value or copy string, so Fast Refresh carries it.
- Changed: `src/components/GracehushTabBar.tsx` (`TabItem`, its constants and its styles), this file (the tree's components line, the Components list, the Navigation Map's two tab bar bullets, this entry), the 08b prompt's appendix (decision 11, B21 to B26) and, outside the repo, the `liquid-glass-tab-bar` skill (what it says of the active tab, its copy of this file and its generic tab bar).
- Verified (no phone): `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint` exit 0. The running dev server compiles the module (one shallow request for that module alone: HTTP 200, with the spring and the three animated styles, and neither `FADE_MS` nor `ACTIVE_SCALE`). A scratch render check of the real `GracehushTabBar` (the repo's TypeScript loader, a fake React, react-native as host names and an Animated whose values the check moves by hand; not in the repo) passed 9 of 9: an inactive tab at rest (the outline icon at 22 over its label, 4 apart, nothing of the active look); the active tab (no label, the filled symbol at 26 in plum, in the middle of the tab, on the lens's own middle line); every twentieth of the way at text sizes 0.88, 1 and 1.3 (the two icons share one middle and one size, their opacities add up to 1, the icon only grows and only comes down, and the label stays at least 3 clear of it while it shows); the icon's way against the label's real height at 0.88, 1, 1.3 and 2 (the cap); a tab change (two tab springs, the tab left to 0 and the tab chosen to 1, on the native driver, critically damped, never past 1, under 0.65 of the way at 150 ms, nine tenths between 240 and 400 ms, landed within 600 ms, and the lens's own spring untouched); a tab chosen mid-change (the running spring stopped, the next one from where the value is, an untouched tab never animated); Reduce Motion (no animation, the values switched); the spoken labels on iOS and Android with the drawing hidden; and pressing (one tick and one navigation for an inactive tab, neither for the active one, the pressed dim and squash, no dock on Scholar). 30 of 30 deliberate breakages, each a copy of the file with one thing broken and served to the check in place of the repo's (the repo file never written), were caught by a named check, among them the label kept on the active tab or drawn again, an active icon no bigger or much bigger, the icon not brought to the middle, the text size or its cap ignored, the 150 ms fade back, a spring that bounces, is fast, is sluggish or runs on the JS driver, Reduce Motion ignored, a running spring not stopped, a label that does not sink or fades over the whole way, either icon left visible, either icon not scaled with the other, a swapped transform list, the drawing open to screen readers, and the lens's spring changed with the tabs'.

The first checks were by hand. From V3 on, at the owner's request to automate the whole step and to be asked only for what needs their hands, the agent drove everything through the dev server's inspector: the test screen's own buttons through their handlers, a made-up sentence sent as text in place of the owner's voice, timings from the screen's recorder, the audio engine's state from read-only native getters, the microphone's send statistics, and ElevenLabs' own record of each talk (lengths and timings, never a word). 30 test talks in all.
- **V1, End: FAIL, fixed, PASS.** End did not end the talk: the SDK switched the audio off before it closed the connection, iOS refused, and the first talk stayed connected for the agent's whole 600 seconds (4,400 credits). With the app's own session setup (vendor note) every later End disconnected in 0.17 to 0.6 s, and the audio session was released on the first try.
- **V2 and V4, talks in a row: FAIL, fixed, PASS.** Only the first talk after the app started heard the owner. The agent's first fix (unmuting the microphone around the connection) was wrong: after a restart the engine reported recording and unmuted in every talk, and still only the first was heard. The cause is the known issue in the vendor note, and the input mixer mute mode fixed it: six talks in one app session were all transcribed, speaking over Scholar stopped it about 0.47 s after the speech began, and an answer started 0.5 to 0.8 s after the owner stopped speaking.
- **V3, slow answers: FAIL, fixed, PASS.** At 3 s of server delay the answer's first sound came 3.7 s after the message. At 6 s ElevenLabs gave up after 12.4 s and ended the talk itself (the agent's 4-second default). With 15 s set in the agent's code, 6 and 10 s of delay gave 6.7 and 10.7 s, in silence and with no error. A comparison at the old 4 seconds showed that an early silent chunk does not extend the limit; the agent was put back to 15 and checked.
- **The agent's other defaults, found on the way and set with the owner's "Go":** no turn of its own after 7 quiet seconds, no request before the person has finished speaking, no sentiment analysis and no topic discovery (17 of 17 checks after the run). In a talk with 20 quiet seconds afterwards, ElevenLabs sent nothing and Scholar said nothing, the talk stayed connected, and a typed question was then answered.
- **V5, the app's own sound around a talk: PASS on what the phone reports.** Right after a talk the rain preview played its 8 seconds and the Welcome sample played. The recorder then ran a 6-second take with sound levels, and the take was discarded (0 recordings before and after). The next talk's microphone sent sound and its question was answered. The owner was asked three times whether the two sounds were heard and did not answer, so that they were audible is not verified.
- **V6, mute: PASS.** In 3 seconds the microphone sent a sound energy of 1.6e-4 unmuted (about 35 KB), exactly 0 muted (468 bytes) and 2.1e-4 unmuted again. A typed question was answered while muted. The talk was ended muted, and the next one started unmuted and sent sound.
- **V7, what ElevenLabs keeps: read, and deletion proven.** Of 28 talks read, none had audio; the 8 newest still held their words and a summary and title written on ElevenLabs' side, and the 20 older had been emptied by ElevenLabs' own sweep, 5 to 45 minutes after each talk; the record of every talk stays listed. A talk just made, still holding its words, read 404 after a DELETE (204 in 3.3 s). With the owner's "delete", all 30 test talks were deleted, and the agent lists none.
- **V8, the phone locked during a talk: PASS on what the phone reports.** The owner's spoken sentence was transcribed (43 characters), and the answer started 0.77 s after the speech ended, with the early-request setting off. Locked for 27 s, the talk stayed connected with no error, the microphone kept sending sound, and a typed question was answered 0.76 s after it was sent, while the app was in the background. After the unlock, End took 0.6 s. Whether the owner heard Scholar from the locked phone was asked and not answered.
- **For `prompts/39`.** (1) The voice service carries both session fixes, and `@elevenlabs/client` becomes a direct dependency, because its `internal` entry is imported. (2) Scholar's first speakable words must reach ElevenLabs within 15 seconds, and a failed turn ends the talk: the voice path needs a time budget of its own (about 12 s), a written line for an answer that is not ready, and a calm screen for a talk the agent ended. (3) A silence is never a turn and nothing is requested early (the agent's settings); what Scholar does when someone says "stop" is to be decided (the test endpoint simply answered again). (4) Privacy: the server deletes each talk at ElevenLabs when it ends, in the background (a delete takes 3 to 12 s); until then ElevenLabs holds the words and a summary written by its own model, which the Privacy Policy and the consent sheet must say; sentiment analysis and topic discovery stay off. (5) The microphone stays open while the phone is locked: the plan decides whether a talk goes on, pauses or ends there, and whether the screen stays awake during a talk. (6) The talk's end should put the app's playback mode back: nothing does today, and a player that sets the mode itself is unaffected. (7) The microphone permission text in `app.json` still speaks only of reflections. (8) The answer's text reaches the phone about 2 s after its sound starts, and a filler chunk would show in it. (9) For the owner to confirm: a GraceHush-only ElevenLabs account, and the three voices.

- **Differences from the plan, each with its reason.**
  1. **The times of a turn** (decisions 16 and 17, revised by measurement; the vendor note has the numbers). The everyday holding line comes after 7 seconds, not 5. The everyday writer has one attempt with the whole 13 seconds, not 5 seconds an attempt. In a heavy conversation the holding lines come after 5 and 13 seconds.
  2. **The cap and the voice switch are applied by the engine after its screening** (`refuse`), where step 6 of the plan applied them before the turn. A hard moment is then answered whatever the cap or the switch, as a typed message's limit comes only after a clear screening.
  3. **A written answer of last resort in `scholar-voice-llm`**, for a hard moment the engine fails or does not finish in time: said, not saved (`voice:fallback:cut` or `voice:fallback:error`). The engine may still save a late answer the person did not hear.
  4. **Decision 23 in full.** A talk's turns are saved as spoken messages, so without more they would have counted in a later typed message's thirty in ten minutes. The engine takes them out (`countTalkTurns`), which costs two more reads only when that count has reached the limit.
  5. A conversation deleted during a talk (`NOT_FOUND` from the engine) gets the ended line; in a heavy conversation the written answer of last resort comes first.
  6. An account that Scholar is closed for during a talk hears the adults-only answer, which reads the support address aloud. The voice pack asks the readers about it.
  7. ElevenLabs' request is read whatever its content type says, and `scholar-voice-end` answers `INVALID_REQUEST` to a body over its limit.
  8. An end call that comes late counts the talk up to that call (never past its own cap), so Part Two must call end at once. An account's next start closes a talk nobody ended, at its last activity. `scholar-voice-end` also marks the talk heavy when its conversation is.
  9. A talk's turn that failed, or that was released at the cap, is a failed spoken message with its words and no recording. Part Two's "Try again" must work for it.
  10. A turn's message id relies on ElevenLabs sending the talk's whole history with every request, which the test run saw; M2 and the walk-through check it.
  11. `turns` is read and then written, so two turns that finish at the same moment can count as one.
  12. `agent_setup.ts` adopts the test run's agent as the default voice's, removes `ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID` and writes `ELEVENLABS_AGENTS` with `--write-ids`. Every override from the phone is off, and `turn_eagerness` is "patient".
  13. **The evaluation's two checks.** The plan's bar "no answer says 'wrote'" became "no answer speaks of what the person wrote or typed" (`saysTheyWrote`): the plain word flagged "Paul wrote this to encourage people". The 20-to-90-word bar counts the reply's words, not a prayer. `voice-pack.md` is written by every `--spoken` run.
  14. **The repeat check** (`SHARED_WAYS` in `output.ts`) also sets aside "on your screen", "calling or texting" and "phone or text": in a talk they are how an answer points to the help line, and they had cost a retry.
  15. `spoken` is a stripped tag (`CHAT_TAGS`), and the `<spoken>` block says that it comes from the app.
  16. The app's copy of the voice contract and the predicted table were added in Part One, so that `contractParity.ts` covers the contract from the start.
  17. A talk's row keeps its real length in `seconds` (at most the table's 1,900), and what the talk costs is worked out when it is read (`billableSeconds`: the smaller of that and the talk's cap, and nothing for a heavy talk), where step 7 of the plan stored the counted number.

**Step 39, Part One — the measurements, and holding lines that are heard when they are sent (2026-11-13).**

- **What happened.** The owner deployed the test stub on the development project ("Done"), and once more after it learned scripted replies (for each turn a list of pieces with their moments). From this PC the scratch driver then held about forty short test talks with the test run's one agent over ElevenLabs' WebSocket: made-up sentences sent as text, each sound burst timed, and the exact characters spoken read from the audio events' `alignment`. Every talk was deleted afterwards (the agent lists none), and no setting of the agent was changed. The rules that came out of it are in the ElevenLabs vendor note ("How ElevenLabs reads a custom LLM's stream").
- **M2 PASS.** With no words for 15 seconds ElevenLabs asks again as a new request (about 16 s after the message), and that request's answer is spoken.
- **M3: a reply with no words ends the talk.** The socket stays open, and at the person's next message the talk closes with error 1002; three attempts with no words end the same way. So a turn of noise keeps its spoken line, and the "silence" option is removed (`voiceRules` is gone).
- **M1 FAIL as built, fixed.** ElevenLabs does not speak a piece when it arrives: its voice starts once it holds about 50 characters and keeps the last words back until more text arrives or the reply ends. A holding line alone was therefore heard only together with the answer (13.6 s after the message for a line sent at 5 s), so in a hard moment the person would have sat in silence for up to 22 seconds. Tried and not enough: a period, an ellipsis, a line break, 160 spaces, one more chunk of "... ", and three short chunks (which cut a line in the middle of a sentence).
- **The fix, a difference from the plan that is the owner's to veto.** Each holding line goes out with twelve ellipses after it in the same piece (`stream.hold`, `HOLD_PAD` in `_shared/voice/sse.ts`, 48 characters: more than ElevenLabs keeps back). Measured, 9 of 9 runs: lines sent at 5 and 13 s were heard at about 5.5 and 13.6 s and the answer sent at 22 s at about 22.6 s, with one request only; the everyday line sent at 7 s was heard at 7.5 s and the not-ready line sent at 13 s at 13.5 s. The ellipses make no sound: a pause of 0 to about 1 s before the next words. No line's words and no time changed, and decision 19's 22 seconds stand (`voiceTiming.heavyTotalMs` 22,000): an answer sent 14 s after the last holding line was still spoken, and ElevenLabs asks again only after 15 s with no new piece. The fallback announced before the measurements, ElevenLabs' own filler (`turn.soft_timeout_config`), was not needed, not switched on and not measured: it would say the same line in an everyday turn and in a hard moment, which decision 16 rules out.
- **Changed.**

**Step 39, Part One — the pad is voiced in three voices (2026-11-13).**

- **What happened.** The owner's "go" to the open item of the entry above: the scripted hard-moment sequence once more in `wise`, `clear`, `deep` and `warm`, with every burst saved as a WAV, each burst described by Gemini, and each talk deleted afterwards (every agent lists none). A small cutter (scratch, not in the repo) split each burst into its loud stretches, so each stretch could be described on its own.
- **What a person would hear** (the lines and the answer arrived at their moments in all four):
  - `wise`: "I’m still here with you" twice, half a second apart: two stretches of speech, 1.2 and 0.9 s, where the text holds the line once, and Gemini heard the words in each cut piece. Then a 0.2 s sound just before the answer.
  - `clear`: "I’m still here with you" at 13.6 s and again at 22.7 s, just before the answer (Gemini, on the whole burst and on the cut piece).
  - `deep`: a non-word ("Mana" or "Manner", 0.3 s at 48% of the burst's peak) about 3 s after "Give me a moment", and a sigh just before the answer.
  - `warm`: clean.
- **Why.** The twelve "... " groups of `HOLD_PAD` reach ElevenLabs' voice at the start of the next burst (or at the end of the line's own), and the voice fills them with sound, in some voices with the words of a nearby line. ElevenLabs' custom LLM page asks for one "... " at the end of a buffer phrase and warns that text run on from an ellipsis can distort the audio (read 2026-11-13; the page says nothing about flushing, SSML or characters stripped before the voice). The loud stretches of the first eight-voice run were the same thing.
- **How it was read.** The loudness of each burst is the fact: there is sound where the plan has a pause. Gemini named the words; it also invented a phrase for the 0.2 s sound in `wise`, so a sound that short is judged by its loudness alone.
- **Result: FAIL.** The pad is not silent. The real handler is not deployed with it, and the voice pack (whose text says a pause of up to a second follows each line) waits for the fix before it goes to the readers.
- **Cost.** Four talks of about 42 s, roughly 1,300 credits, and 19 short descriptions on Gemini (their usage was not logged; well under a dollar).
- **The first fix tried: 48 zero-width spaces** (`"\u200B".repeat(48)`; the owner's "go"; one talk in `wise`, deleted). Silent: the loudness is flat where they sit, between the two lines and at the start of the answer, and Gemini heard only the words and silence. Not counted: "I’m here. Give me a moment." was spoken at 13.6 s, together with the second line, so the first line came 8 s late. Stopped there, as the stop rule said (about 300 credits).
- **The second fix: sixteen zero-width words** (`HOLD_PAD = "\u200B ".repeat(16)`, a zero-width space and an ordinary space, sixteen times; the owner's "GO"). One talk in `wise`, then every other voice once and `wise`, `clear` and `deep` a second time: 11 talks, each deleted (every agent lists none).
  - **Counted:** every opening line as written, the first holding line's sound at 5.4 to 5.9 s after the message, the second's at 13.5 to 13.9 s and the answer's at 22.6 to 22.9 s.
  - **Silent:** in all 33 bursts Gemini heard exactly the expected words and nothing else, and the loudness shows no stretch but the words, save one trace: in 4 of the 11 talks (`wise` twice, `bright` and `soft`) ElevenLabs kept the first line's period back with the pad, and the second line's burst begins with a stretch of 30 to 60 ms (a mean loudness of at most 23% of the burst's peak), a tick before the line. ElevenLabs' character timings show the held-back period in exactly those four.
  - **Why it works:** ElevenLabs' buffer counts words separated by ordinary spaces. Twelve dot-words were counted, one run of 48 zero-width spaces was not, and sixteen zero-width words are, while the voice has nothing in them to say.
- **Result: PASS**, with the tick as a known limit.
- **Built.** `HOLD_PAD` in `_shared/voice/sse.ts`, and its test in `sse_test.ts`: sixteen words, none of them a letter, a number, a mark or a symbol, and every holding line with its pad at least eighteen words. The handler's tests read a reply as before and now also refuse a piece that carries part of the pad as zero-width spaces (they looked only for dots). The docs: the ElevenLabs vendor note, the `scholar-voice-llm` rule and its sentence on the times, the plan, and the voice pack's text in `run_scholar_eval.ts` and in `scholar-eval/voice-pack.md`, which may now go to the readers. Its recordings hold each holding line alone, without the pad, so they need no new sounds.
- **Measured (no phone).** `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint` exit 0, and the release gate prints nothing. Deno: every `check` clean (each function also with its own `deno.json`), lint 198 files, fmt 228 files, the main test run 971 passed and export-data's 27; parity 8 of 8. Breakages, in a scratch copy of the functions and never the repo (control 188 over 16 test files): the 9 that touch the pad, each caught by a named test: no pad, the pad as one run of zero-width spaces, the twelve ellipses back, eight zero-width words, a holding line sent with only part of its pad (caught by the handler's own reading of the reply), the pad on every piece of an answer, the everyday and the second heavy holding line said with no pad, and a holding line counted as a piece of the answer.
- **Cost.** The 11 talks, roughly 3,400 credits by the test run's rate, and 33 short descriptions on Gemini (their usage was not logged; well under a dollar).

**Scholar's Talk screen: a voice orb and three controls (2026-11-15).**

- What happened: the owner sent two screenshots, the Talk screen as step 39 built it and a reference voice-agent screen, and said the built page did not look premium and modern and could pass for AI slop. They asked what a top consumer-app team would build, suggested an audio-reactive 3D orb in GraceHush's colours in place of the logo, and three controls with the middle microphone as mute and unmute. One recommendation, "a sound-reactive orb, three controls, nothing else", was approved as written.
- Cause, read from the old page: the brand mark in a white circle sat in a halo that pulsed on two fixed beats (2 seconds while listening, 1.3 while speaking), so nothing on it followed what was being said; the controls were Mute and a crisis-red End, with an X beside the title.
- Decisions (the recommendation's; none struck): (1) The orb, as screen specification 11 describes it: a plum sphere with two slow ribbons of light, a sheen and a rose glow, five bitmap layers drawn from the brand tokens and screen-blended inside the circle. It is a layered 2D orb and not a 3D engine: a real 3D orb needs Skia or GL, which is a new dependency and the owner's to approve, so nothing was installed. (2) It follows the sound through LiveKit's native multiband volume processor (the one LiveKit's own hook makes), for Scholar's track and the person's microphone. Each report runs a small handler that eases the level into Animated values on the native driver, so there is no React render and no per-frame JavaScript. The level is the root mean square of the five bands stretched from a floor of 0.08 to a ceiling of 0.6 (`orbLevel`), taken at once when it rises and let fall by 15% a report when it drops (`settleLevel`: half in about 200 ms, at rest in about a second). (3) The screen finds the two tracks in the LiveKit room behind ElevenLabs' conversation (the vendor note). A talk whose room cannot be reached still turns and breathes: it only loses the reaction to the voice. (4) Three controls: Hold, the microphone (mute and unmute) and End. Hold is new: it mutes the microphone and sends the typed turn "Wait." (the server's stop word), and Resume unmutes and sends "Okay, go on." (the recap), so it needs no server change. The microphone button waits while the talk is held. (5) End is white and not crisis red, which revises the plan's decision 8: nothing is wrong when a talk ends, and the page now has no red. (6) The header is the title and the voice's name. The X went, because End does the same, and the AI line moved from under the header to above the controls, smaller, to give the orb the middle. (7) In a heavy conversation the orb is smaller, the help line stays on screen under it and there is no countdown, as the plan's decision 40 says. (8) No haptic, event or log line for Hold, Resume or Mute. (9) New files, classes and assets: restart the dev server with `npx expo start -c --dev-client`.
- Added: `src/components/scholar/VoiceOrb.tsx`, `src/utils/orbLevel.ts`, the five orb PNGs in `assets/images/` and their keys in `images.ts`. Changed: `src/screens/scholar/ScholarTalkScreen.tsx` (rewritten), `src/services/scholarTalk.ts` (`held`, `setTalkHeld`, and the microphone waits while held), `src/constants/app.ts` (the two typed turns), `src/constants/copy.ts` (`talk.voice`, `status.held`, `hold` and `resume`; `talk.close` removed), `src/hooks/usePulse.ts` (a comment) and `supabase/tests/scholar/run.cjs` (five checks, 63 in all). Not touched: the server, a migration, `package.json`, `app.json`, the tokens and every other screen.
- The images are drawn by a PIL script from the brand tokens, not by an image model. The script is in the session's scratchpad and not in the repo, so this is its record. `orb-core.png` (512): a radial fill from `plum` at the centre to `plum-deep` from 55% of the radius, a touch lighter at the top left. `orb-ribbon-rose.png` (512): an ellipse of `rose` (150 by 85, 28 degrees, peak 0.9, blurred 28). `orb-ribbon-light.png` (512): an ellipse of `terracotta` mixed 45% into `glass` (130 by 75, minus 40 degrees, peak 0.85, blurred 26). `orb-sheen.png` (512): white (118 by 72, minus 35 degrees, peak 0.5, blurred 22). `orb-glow.png` (640): `rose` at 80% in the middle, falling to nothing at the edge. All are RGBA with no metadata, nothing is drawn on the border (alpha 0 there, read back), and together they weigh 113,944 bytes.
- Measured (no phone): `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint` exit 0 (run one at a time with `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=2048`); the release gate prints nothing; every Node suite at its count: scholar 63 (58 and the five new), profile-sync 93, journal-data 104, ai-permission 16, notifications 51, deletion 36, offline 44 of 44, recording 68, playback 135, ambient 64, prayers 34, billing 24, account 23, realtime 27, analytics 36 and affirmations 13; parity 8 of 8. The five new checks are Hold and Resume against the service (the microphone, the typed words, only while live, the clock running on), the level and how it settles, the server's stop word recognising Hold and not Resume (read from `stop.ts`), and two source checks, one on the screen and one on the orb. A scratch render check of the real screen and orb outside the repo (the repo's TypeScript loader, a one-pass React with the real `useMemo` and a subscribing `useSyncExternalStore`, react-native as host names, a recording Animated, and fakes of the ElevenLabs provider and the talk service) passed 31 of 31: the header, the three controls in every state with their labels and disabling, the status text and its live region, each orb state's dimming, glow, ring and breath, the level following the right track and the crossover, the processor made and deleted with its track, Reduce Motion, the heavy layout, the failed and ended views, and the room store's events and cleanup. 111 deliberate breakages in a scratch copy of the repo (never the repo; the copy equalled it before and after): 109 caught by a named check and 2 equivalent, left as they are. One removes the `liveKitNative()` guard, which changes nothing a person can see, because the call is inside a `try` that returns quietly; the other removes the ring's cleanup `setValue(1)`, because the next effect run starts with the same line. The running dev server compiled `VoiceOrb.tsx`, `ScholarTalkScreen.tsx`, `orbLevel.ts` and `images.ts` (HTTP 200, each with its expected contents) and served the five PNGs byte for byte. No `expo export` was run: the owner's dev server holds the memory.
- Verified against the installed sources, not on a phone: LiveKit's call and event contract, the 64 dB scale, and the path from ElevenLabs' conversation to the room (the vendor note has all three).
- Not verified: everything on a phone. How the orb looks (five screen-blended bitmap layers under Fabric on an iPhone XR, the sphere's edge and the glow's reach). Whether LiveKit's processor reports for both tracks on the phone, the local microphone's in particular, and what it reports in a quiet room and at a full voice, which sets the floor and the ceiling (`getOrbLevelDebug()` in a development build shows it). Whether a typed "Wait." interrupts an answer that is already being spoken. The battery and heat cost of two processors at about 25 reports a second each, with a screen-blended orb, over a long talk. Android, VoiceOver and TalkBack, and 320 wide at the largest text size.
- Known limits: the orb is layered 2D, not 3D. The glow fades to about 19% of its own opacity at three quarters of its radius, so the scrolling middle's edge can clip it faintly in a heavy talk or at large text. Each Resume is an ordinary turn, so it spends one of the talk's 80 turns and one model call. A talk whose room cannot be reached has an orb that moves with its state only. `getOrbLevelDebug()` exists in development builds only.
- Phone walk-through: not run yet. B0 the state: restart the dev server with `npx expo start -c --dev-client`, force-quit and reopen the app, a Pro account with the voice permission given, `voiceSupported()` true. B1 a talk opens: the title with the voice's name, the orb connecting with a ring leaving it, Hold and the microphone dimmed and End live, read from the tree and `getOrbLevelDebug().native`. - Decisions (the agent's, on the owner's request; none asked again):
  1. The model is `src/utils/orbShape.ts`, pure. The outline is a circle plus four travelling waves of two, three, four and five lobes: at rest 0.6%, 0.4%, 0.3% and 0.2% of the radius (1.5% in all), and a full voice adds 3.4%, 2.6%, 1.8% and 1.4% (`LOBE_VOICE`; 4% for the broadest lobe made a loud voice squash the sphere in the preview). Low bands drive the broad lobes and high bands the fine ones. At rest the waves travel at 0.5, 0.7, 0.9 and 1.2 radians a second, alternating in direction, and a full voice makes them three times as fast. A voice is followed with a rise of 35 ms and a fall of 120 ms on the UI thread, after LiveKit's reports have settled (`settleDrive`, the level's rule per band). A change of voice takes about 70 ms and a change of state about 100 ms. A frame longer than 50 ms moves the orb only 50 ms, and every angle is kept within one turn.
  2. The look is `src/components/scholar/orbShader.ts`, one SkSL string. From the back it draws the rose glow (gone before the canvas's edge), a plum ring that keeps the outline's shape, then the sphere: plum to plum-deep, lighter at the top left, two ribbons of light through a slow liquid warp, a white sheen and a rose rim. Every colour is a token or made from them (a check compares plum, plum-deep and rose with the tokens).
  3. `src/components/scholar/VoiceOrbSkia.tsx` steps the model once a frame on the UI thread (`useFrameCallback`, `stepOrb` with `modify`, `orbUniforms`) and hands the uniforms to the shader as a shared value. The canvas is 1.6 times the sphere and centred on it. A report or a frame renders nothing in React.
  4. LiveKit's ears moved to `src/components/scholar/voiceLevels.ts`, shared by the two renderers. Each report becomes [level, low, mid, high], settled there and handed to the drawn orb's sink. `getOrbLevelDebug()` now also says which orb is drawn (`renderer`).
  5. `VoiceOrb.tsx` chooses once, when the Talk screen first loads it. It draws the shader orb when Skia's native module is in the build and the shader compiles, and the first orb (five bitmap layers, unchanged) otherwise: Expo Go, a build from before 2026-11-15, or a shader that does not compile. Skia's JavaScript is required only in the first case, because it throws on load without its module.
  6. Only what runs in the frame is a worklet. The report side runs on the JavaScript thread, where LiveKit's events arrive.

**Share opens the chat app it went to (2026-11-16).**

They asked that the person land in the app they shared to, to see what they sent, with GraceHush left in the background to come back to. iOS runs a share extension inside the app that shares and closes it back into that app after sending, so GraceHush cannot keep the person there: it can only open that app itself once the share is done.
- Decision (the agent's, on the owner's request): when `Share.share` resolves `sharedAction`, the app iOS names (`activityType`, the share extension's bundle id) is matched by the start of that id (`src/utils/shareReturn.ts`: WhatsApp, Telegram, Messenger, Facebook, X, Instagram, LinkedIn and Signal), and `openAppAfterShare` opens it by its URL scheme with no path (`whatsapp://` and so on), so it shows its own last screen. Messages, Mail, Notes, Copy, AirDrop and every app not listed stay in GraceHush. A dismissed sheet opens nothing. Android reports no app (React Native resolves `activityType: null` there), so nothing changes on Android. Reflection's verse share does the same. No `canOpenURL` (it needs declared schemes, a native change); `openURL` alone needs none, so no new build. Considered and not built: a share menu of the app's own with direct targets (WhatsApp's own picker, then the chat), which would replace the system sheet and its contact suggestions.

**Scholar welcomes a greeting (scholar-v3, 2026-11-16).**

- What happened: the owner said "Hello" to Scholar and got a pleasant reply that named nothing GraceHush is for. They asked that the reply speak of what the app is for, as the Journal's filter names it (anxiety, weariness, grief, hopelessness, a need for prayer), so a person believes the app is built for what they are going through and is glad to share it.
- Decisions (the agent's, on the owner's request; no question asked):
  1. A rule in Scholar's instruction, not a canned reply: the model writes the welcome, so it follows any form of greeting and is worded freshly.
  2. When the new message only greets Scholar, asks what it can do, or says the person is not sure where to begin, and nothing earlier says what they need, the answer welcomes them. It says they can bring whatever they carry today, names worry and anxiety, feeling worn out, grief, a hope that feels far away, needing prayer and questions about the Bible, says what Scholar can do (listen, look at Scripture, pray with them), and asks in one short question what is on their heart, a few words being enough. At most 70 words, with no passage and no prayer, and never "safe" or "private": that promise belongs to the Privacy Policy, not to a model.
  3. The writer marks a welcome with `welcome`, right after `is_heavy`, in both everyday schemas (typed and spoken); the heavy schema has none. `parseScholarReply` keeps only a welcome's words: no title, so the next answer titles the conversation, and no passage. A reply that prays is no welcome, because the person asked for prayer and the prayer stands.
  4. The server saves `welcome` in the answer's content and answers it on each message (`ScholarMessage.welcome`, both contract copies), never in a heavy conversation.
  5. Under a welcome the chips are the situations, as the Journal's filter names them, each sent as the person's own first words: "I’m feeling anxious", "I’m feeling weary", "I’m grieving", "I need hope" and "I need prayer". It is "I need hope" and not "I’m losing hope", which the screening could read as a risk. Under any other answer the chips are the three ways to go further, as before.
  6. Added after the evaluation: a request for prayer with nothing in the conversation saying what for (the chip "I need prayer") is prayed at once, for whatever they carry today and without guessing what it is, and the reply invites them to say more (one sentence in the Prayer section). That condition never holds in a hard moment, which always says what it is about.
  7. The app reads a missing `welcome` as false, and an older app ignores the field, so the deploy and the build can come in either order.
  8. `SCHOLAR_PROMPT_VERSION` is `scholar-v3` (a talk's `scholar-v3/spoken-v4`).
  9. No migration, package, secret or analytics event. The only copy is the five chips.

**Share to WhatsApp lands in the chosen chat (2026-11-16).**

- What happened: the owner shared an answer to a WhatsApp contact through the system share sheet, and GraceHush then opened WhatsApp on the chat they had been in before, not the one they shared to. iOS reports only which share extension took the text (`activityType`), never the chat, so opening WhatsApp afterwards could only show its last screen. The recommendation, approved with "Go ahead": GraceHush's own share sheet, with WhatsApp's own chat picker.
- Decisions:
  1. A tap on Share (Scholar's answers, Reflection's verse) opens `ShareSheet` when the phone has WhatsApp: a blush `BottomSheet` with one "Share" group of two `SettingsRow`s, WhatsApp ("Choose a chat, then tap Send", with the external mark) and More ways to share ("Messages, Mail, Copy and more"). A phone without WhatsApp gets the system share sheet at once, so nobody taps through a sheet with one row.
  2. WhatsApp opens `whatsapp://send?text=` with the whole message encoded (`whatsAppShareUrl`): WhatsApp's picker, the person chooses a chat, lands in it with the text typed, and taps Send there. When WhatsApp cannot be opened, the system share sheet opens with the same message.
  3. Each choice goes on after the sheet has gone: on iOS from its `onDismiss`, or after `MODAL_HANDOFF_FALLBACK_MS` if iOS never reports it, once; on Android at once. iOS cannot present the system share sheet while another Modal is leaving.
  4. Whether the phone has WhatsApp is `Linking.canOpenURL("whatsapp://send")`, which needs `LSApplicationQueriesSchemes: ["whatsapp"]` in app.json's Info.plist and so reaches a phone only with a new build. A development build always offers WhatsApp (`__DEV__`) and falls back when it is not there. Android needs a `<queries>` entry that no build has, so it answers false there and goes straight to the system sheet.
  5. The app opened after the system sheet (`shareReturn.ts`, `openAppAfterShare`, earlier the same day) is gone, so Messages, Mail, Telegram and the rest behave as iOS does.
  6. Unchanged: what is shared (Scholar's words first, then its verified passages; the verse alone on Reflection), never in a heavy conversation or under an answer with a help line, no haptic, no event, nothing logged. Nothing installed. WhatsApp's row has a plain chat bubble, not WhatsApp's logo (no brand file was added).

**Scholar's conversation history: three on the tab, the rest behind See all (2026-11-16).**

- What happened: the owner looked at the Scholar tab's "Recent conversations" list (the newest 30 in one card) and asked how a top consumer app would handle a person with a hundred conversations. One recommendation was approved with "Go".
- Cause: the tab asked for the newest 30 and drew them all, so the list grew until it pushed the starters' neighbours and the AI line far down the page, with no way to find an older conversation and no end to the scroll.
- Decisions (the recommendation's; none struck): (1) The tab shows the latest three, with a plum "See all" on the heading row only when more exist (it asks for four to know). (2) The Conversations screen (screen specification 9b) is a push above the tabs: a search pill, sticky groups (Today, Yesterday, Previous 7 days, then a heading for each month), 30 a page loaded on scroll in a virtualised list, a skeleton and the empty, no-result and error states. (3) The search runs on the server by title (`ILIKE`, no migration), so it covers every conversation; a conversation with no title (a heavy one) never matches and is listed as before. (4) Delete is a long press (and a screen reader action) opening the app's own sheet and then the existing confirmation, online only, never queued; no swipe, because that would be the first use of `react-native-gesture-handler` and needs approval. (5) Nothing is cached on the phone, and the screen makes no haptic, event or log line. (6) JavaScript only: no migration, server change, package or native change.
- Added: `src/screens/scholar/ScholarHistoryScreen.tsx`, `src/hooks/useScholarHistory.ts`, `src/utils/scholarHistory.ts`. Changed: `ScholarScreen.tsx` (the heading row and "See all"), `useScholarHome.ts` (`hasMore`), `scholarRepository.ts` (`listConversations({ limit, cursor?, query? })` answers a page), `scholarRemote.ts` (`selectConversationPage`), `data/mock/scholar.ts` (`pageMockConversations`), `navigation/types.ts` and `RootNavigator.tsx` (the `ScholarHistory` route), `constants/app.ts` (`SCHOLAR_HOME_RECENTS` 3, `SCHOLAR_HISTORY_PAGE` 30, `SCHOLAR_SEARCH_DEBOUNCE_MS` 350 in place of `SCHOLAR_RECENTS_LIMIT`), `constants/copy.ts` (`copy.scholar.history`), `utils/format.ts` (`formatClock`), and the checks: the fake PostgREST of `supabase/tests/journal-data/world.cjs` gained `ilike` (case-insensitive, `%`, `_` and a backslash as Postgres reads them, a null never matches) and `supabase/tests/scholar/run.cjs` 12 checks (88 in all). Each file kept its line endings.
- Differences from what a first draft would do, each found while building: (a) the cursor is the last row's time exactly as the server wrote it, because cutting it to milliseconds would skip the rows between it and the next millisecond (a check holds `lt.` to the server's own text); (b) the focus refresh merges the first page into the pages already loaded (`mergeFirstPage`) instead of replacing them, so coming back from a conversation does not throw the person back to the top, and a conversation deleted meanwhile drops out; (c) the refs the hook keeps are written only inside callbacks, never during render, which the React Compiler lint rules refuse; (d) the sheet keeps its title while it slides out (a separate open flag), so the title does not flip to "A conversation with Scholar" mid-animation.
- Measured (no phone): `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint` exit 0 (with `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=3072`: earlier attempts had crashed with out-of-memory while the host's committed memory sat at its limit, 65,214 of 65,394 MB, with the processes themselves holding about 16 GB; nothing in the code was wrong). **The Today tab, polish pass: the week appears when it is earned, a quieter Listen again, a taller word card and one rhythm (2026-11-17).**

- What happened: the owner sent a screenshot of the Today tab (an account whose newest reflection was a week old) with the week strip circled: seven blank rings. They asked how it improves the UI, whether users will care, and how the screen can be more premium. The honest answer: as drawn it added nothing, it was the weakest element, seven near-invisible petal rings read as an unfinished widget and as a quiet "you did nothing", and it sat tight under the greeting. One recommendation, five changes, was approved with "Go ahead".
- Decisions (the recommendation's; none struck, one deviation below): (1) **The strip is drawn only once one of its seven days is filled** (`weekDots.some((dot) => dot.reflected)` in `JournalFeedScreen.tsx`): with nothing filled the greeting stands alone, and the strip appears the first time a day is filled, as something earned. The week is worked out once and handed to the strip. **The Word Deck: the lock screen plays the words of every reflection of the week (2026-11-17).**

- What happened: the owner asked what happens to the lock screen when a person makes several reflections in a week or in a day. The planner drew all 21 notifications (7 days times 3) from the single newest reflection (`readCachedAffirmationSource` and `planAffirmations`), so the same three words repeated for seven days and a new reflection replaced every pending one; Today's word card read the same way. The owner asked for a workflow that covers all the reflections of the week and keeps three notifications a day, built the way the large consumer apps build a daily-return loop, asked for a summary of the implementation, rules and psychology first, and approved it with "Go ahead and Implement it".
- Decisions (the recommendation's; none struck): (1) exactly three notifications a day at the three reminder times, planned 7 days ahead (21 of iOS's 64), never more, and the app still goes quiet 7 days after it was last opened, with no nagging. (2) The pool is every word (a headline with its verse) of the reflections of the last 7 local calendar days, the newest 14 at most, a heavy moment since 2026-11-08 included; a week with fewer than 7 reflections is topped up with older ones to 7. (3) The deal, in time order: each reminder goes to the reflection that has waited longest for a turn (never-turned first, so a new reflection plays at the next reminder; a tie goes to the week before older ones, then to the newer), and inside it to the word that has waited longest (never-dealt first, then the word whose own slot is the delivery slot, then the order: the model's best three in day order, then the added ones by position). A word never repeats until its reflection's others have been heard. (4) Today's card shows the word of the reminder that last fired (from the same calendar, so it works with notifications off and agrees with the lock screen); a tap opens that word's own reflection on its Affirmations tab and never starts audio. (5) Safety unchanged: a notification carries a headline and a verse only, never the person's words, names or danger; a verse-less word keeps "{Slot} affirmation" with the headline as the body, the slot being the delivery slot; a legacy heavy moment (saved before 2026-11-08, words only) as the newest finished entry keeps the quiet it always imposed; deleting a reflection removes its words at the next plan; a reminder-time or time-zone change deals the upcoming reminders again. (6) Costs accepted: JavaScript only; one local table `word_calendar` (schema version 4, ids and times only, wiped with the database file at sign-out); no server, migration, package or native change; no new copy and no new analytics event. (7) Psychology taken, with the rule that keeps each honest: variety and a fresh word at the right time (a pattern the person can predict), the newest reflection heard at the very next reminder (the work they just did is acknowledged at once), a new word every time with no repeat until the deck is used up, and one card that matches the lock screen. Refused, because AGENTS.md forbids it: guilt or loss-framed streaks, escalating pings, scarcity or countdowns, promised outcomes, and any claim about privacy or safety. (8) Not in this change, each its own yes: a heart raising a word's priority, and a "Next word · 1:00 PM" line on Today.

- What happened: the owner asked whether GraceHush is profitable at the paywall as it stood ($59.99 a year, $9.99 a month, a 7-day trial on the yearly plan) once Apple's cut, the API costs and the Arcads and Higgsfield subscriptions are counted, then sent screenshots of Hallow's paywall (a hard paywall before sign-in, "Design Your Trial"). The agent built a scratch model (not kept: every input is an assumption or a benchmark, except the API unit costs, which come from this file; Subscription Rules has the numbers) and gave one recommendation, approved with "Implement your Recommendation (one plan)". The owner added that the phone check must be automated: the agent does the work and asks the owner only to tap, lock the phone or reload.
- Decisions (the recommendation's; none struck): (1) Launch prices are $69.99 a year (selected first, a 7-day free trial, the 55% saving the Paywall computes from the fetched prices) and $12.99 a month with no trial. The owner creates the products in App Store Connect, Play Console and RevenueCat; no price or product id is in code, and `data/mock/offerings.ts` kept its placeholder prices (changed the same evening, below). (2) Value-first as built (3 free devotionals a week, then the paywall): no hard paywall yet. (3) The US storefront only at launch, and Apple's Small Business Program before the first sale (15% instead of 30% while proceeds stay under $1 million a year). (4) A trial-end reminder, the one feature of the plan that needed code (below). (5) Organic posting and the tools only until a paying subscriber costs less than the Content Strategy Brief's range. (6) Not built, each needing the owner's yes: a hidden fair-use cap of 3 devotionals a day on Pro (it conflicts with the Paywall row "Unlimited audio devotionals" and needs a Terms sentence and a server change), a hard-paywall variant and a paid 30-day trial of about $2.99 (both to be tested with RevenueCat Experiments once there is traffic).
- The reminder's design: a local notification, no push and no server. (1) **When:** 10:00 on the person's own clock, two calendar days before the day the trial ends, which is 38 to 62 hours before the end (an hour more or less where the clocks change), so about a day is left to act: Apple lets a trial be cancelled up to 24 hours before it ends and no later. It is scheduled only when the trial ends in the future, the reminder moment is at least `TRIAL_REMINDER_MIN_LEAD_MS` (10 s) ahead and the trial is at least `TRIAL_REMINDER_MIN_TRIAL_DAYS` (3) long. (2) **Words** (revised the same evening, below): the title names the weekday the trial ends, and the body what is kept, what the plan costs after the trial and where to manage it, the same on both platforms, built by hand from the zone's own calendar, with curly punctuation. (3) **The row:** `TrialReminderRow` under the plan cards in the scrolling page and never in the pinned block, so the plans keep the place the fold pass of 2026-11-15 gave them; "Remind me before my trial ends" over "One notification, about two days before it ends."; shown only when the selected plan has a trial of three days or more that the store confirmed for this person and the phone can show notifications (`canOfferTrialReminder`: a permission never asked is fine, a refused one hides the row); on by default; a changed value ticks `selection` once (the hook ticks, not the row). (4) **The purchase:** a trial purchase with the switch on schedules the reminder, even if the screen has closed meanwhile; the OS permission is asked then, in context; the done view adds one calm line about what became of it ("We’ll remind you on Saturday, Nov 28, before your trial ends.", or that notifications are off, or that it could not be set); a reminder that is refused or fails never fails the purchase. (5) **The end** comes from RevenueCat (`trialStatusFromCustomerInfo`: an active `pro` in its trial period with an expiration date); the entitlement store holds `trial: { endsAt, willRenew }`, cleared at sign-out and for another account; the mock data source's trial ends after its seven days. (6) **The plan watch** follows RevenueCat's answer for the signed-in account on the real data source only, once for each answer (`reconcileTrialReminder`): a trial that is gone, or was cancelled in the store and will not renew, has its waiting reminder removed and a shown one dismissed (only `trial-ending`: see the revision below); an active renewing trial is left alone with no call at all; it never creates a reminder and never asks for a permission. (7) **Sign-out and account deletion** clear it right after the affirmations and before the plan watch stops. (8) **The tap** opens the Profile tab (`MainTabs` with `pop: true`), is held until the signed-in screens are up and acted on once for each delivery (the key is the identifier and the delivery date), and never starts audio. (9) Nothing is reported anywhere: no analytics event, and in development only a failed step is logged. (10) Its identifier is `trial-ending` (the developer test `trial-test-{ms}`), everything of ours starts with `trial-`, so a clean-up never touches an affirmation or another project's notification. (11) Nothing installed; no server, migration, secret, `app.json` or native change.

- Breakages, in a scratch copy of the repo with a junction to `node_modules` (never the repo; a clean control of all six suites first): **91 of 91 caught by a named check.** The first run caught 88; the three survivors were gaps in the checks, not in the code, and were closed and re-run alone: an answer that was already there when the plan watch starts is reconciled once at the start (a new billing check), a trial bought where the switch was not offered makes no reminder (the paywall check now buys a trial with `canOffer` false and with the trial unconfirmed), and the row itself is disabled while a purchase runs (the screen check now reads the row's own element). The tap check was also made exact (the same delivery twice opens Profile once, a later one opens it again): its old assertion, "at most two", passed a double open. One condition, `result.tier === "trial"` in the hook, is defence in depth: a trial's end is set by a trial purchase only, so the condition cannot change an outcome and was not counted as a survivor. The breakage runner is in the session's scratchpad, not the repo.
- Revised the same evening, on the owner's objection (twice): the first wording told people how to avoid being charged and by when ("To avoid being charged, cancel by Sunday, Nov 29 at 3:00 PM in your App Store settings."), and the owner said a reminder should encourage people to stay subscribed, as the large apps' reminders do, and that this one made the app sound not worth paying for. They were right: the reminder's job here is to keep the value in view, not to hand over the exit. The words are now value-first (Notification Rules has them): the title "Your GraceHush trial ends Monday" and the body "Keep unlimited devotionals and longer Scholar conversations. After your trial, Pro continues at $69.99 per year. Tap to manage your plan.", with the price and the period the bought package's own, no cancel deadline, no clock time and no store named, the same on both platforms. Kept honest: the Paywall's disclosure still names where to cancel (both stores require it), the reminder states the price (the person is told what they will pay), and nothing is promised or pressed. `TrialTerms` (`price`, `period`) travels from the Paywall to the service; an empty price schedules nothing; the developer panel's test reads its terms from the current offering's yearly package.

**Scholar for paying Pro, its credits, and the launch pricing revised (2026-11-18 and 2026-11-19).**

- What happened: the evening of 2026-11-18 the owner's product manager proposed new launch prices ($14.99 a month and $125.99 a year, a 3-day free trial on the yearly plan), Scholar for Pro only, and Scholar credits that renew 24 hours after their first use, with a countdown in the chat. They replace the morning's $69.99 and $12.99 (the entry above). The owner decided "Dont includes Scholar for Free trial": the trial covers the devotionals, and Scholar opens when the paid plan begins. The owner asked for numbers that do not make Pro look stingy, and approved the build with "Go ahead and Implement payment and all 3 recommendations". The three recommendations: (1) Scholar's messages and Listen spend credits, 400 in a window of 24 hours from the first spend (a message 4, an answer read aloud 3 for every 100 characters of its script); (2) the live talk keeps its own time, 60 minutes a calendar month (30 before) and at most 10 minutes a talk; (3) the app shows the credits as a percentage left, never as a number. The profit model given with it is under Subscription Rules ("The model behind it"): assumptions, except the API unit costs.
- Decisions (the recommendation's; none struck):
  1. **Prices** as Subscription Rules has them; no price or product id in code. `data/mock/offerings.ts` holds them as the preview's placeholders: $125.99 with a 3-day trial ("Save 30%", $10.50 a month, computed) and $14.99 with none. The mock trial ends after the offering's free days.
  2. **Scholar is part of a paying Pro plan alone.** The composer is never closed, and the plan is checked after the safety screening (`confirmPaidPlan`, then `checkMessage` in `_shared/scholar/usage.ts`). A free account's or a trial's clear message is saved as failed with `LIMIT_REACHED` and `usage.kind` `scholar_plan` (`resetsAt` null for a free account; for a trial, the day its plan begins). Try again answers it once the plan includes Scholar. A free account sees "Scholar is part of GraceHush Pro. Your message is saved." with See plans (the Paywall, source `scholar`, reason `messages`). A trial sees "Scholar opens when your plan begins on {day}. Your message is saved." and no paywall.
  3. **A heavy conversation** is answered on every plan, never counted, has `usage` null and no credits line, and anyone may listen there (Crisis Safety Rules are unchanged).
  4. **Credits on the server:** `SCHOLAR_CREDITS` (`_shared/scholar/constants.ts`), migration 15's `scholar_credits` and `spend_scholar_credits` (Database Rules). A message is answered while any credit is left, so its cost may take the window past its allowance. The spend runs after the response, and each answer's `usage` is the credits once its message is spent (`creditsAfterSpend`).
  5. **Listen:** `checkListen` refuses an account that is not Pro on every part (`listen_plan`; for a trial, `resetsAt` is the day its plan begins). Pro's credits are checked on part 0 only, and part 0 pays `listenCost` of the whole script after its response.
  6. **The talk:** an account that is not Pro, a trial included, is refused with `talk_plan`, in a heavy conversation too (`_shared/voice/allowance.ts`). `VOICE_LIMITS.monthSeconds` is 3,600.
  7. **The app:**
     - The credits are read once when a conversation opens, and only for an account RevenueCat calls Pro (`readScholarCredits`). After that they come from each answer's `usage`, and a read that comes back after an answer never replaces the answer's numbers.
     - At `SCHOLAR_CREDITS_LOW_PERCENT` (20) or less, a line shows ("Scholar credits: 15% left · renews in 6 h 12 min", the percent and the minutes rounded up).
     - With none left: "You’ve used today’s Scholar credits." with "They renew in …" under it, moved every `SCHOLAR_CREDITS_TICK_MS` (30 s).
     - Neither is a live region, and neither shows in a heavy conversation.
     - Listen and Talk on a trial say "Scholar opens when your plan begins on {day}." from RevenueCat's trial (`useEntitlement`'s `trialEndsAt`); on a free account they open the Paywall. The Talk screen shows a trial's `talk_plan` refusal with Close and no Try again.
     - The Scholar tab's hero marks its button Pro for a trial too, and a trial's tap opens a conversation.
  8. **`SCHOLAR_FREE_DAILY_BUDGET`** is no longer read, and its name left `.env.example`. `scholar_usage` still records each person's messages and listens of the day, and nothing reads it as a limit.
  9. **The words, value-first, and none says how to leave:**
     - The Paywall's Scholar row is "Scholar, your Bible companion" (it was "Longer conversations with Scholar"), and its Scholar banner "Scholar is part of GraceHush Pro."
     - A line under the plans while the selected plan has a trial: "Your free trial includes unlimited devotionals. Scholar opens when your plan begins."
     - A trial's done and member views say when Scholar opens.
     - The trial-end reminder's body begins "Keep unlimited devotionals, and Scholar opens when your plan begins."
  10. **The log line:** `limit` is `free_blocked`, `trial_blocked`, `pro_ok`, `pro_blocked` or `exempt`, with no zone suffix. `limitUsed` is the credits used (null outside Pro). There is no new field (43).
  11. Nothing installed; no `app.json`, native or secret change.

- What happened: the owner sent a screenshot of a Scholar conversation and asked for three things: a way to change Scholar's voice inside the chat, a Christian name for each of the eight voices so a person feels the voice is a Christian one, and a small portrait for each that matches how the voice sounds ("a female voice should have an attractive female avatar"), with image prompts they generate and save in the project's Images folder. They generated the eight portraits the same day. It reverses the rule of 2026-11-13 that the voices have no personas, photos or people's names; the Instructional Memory bullet now says so.
- Decisions (the agent's, on the owner's request; none asked again):
  1. The names, one per key, real Christian names from Scripture or church tradition chosen for how each voice sounds: Hannah (`warm`, the default: the woman whose prayer was heard, 1 Samuel 1), Phoebe (`bright`: her name means bright, Romans 16:1), Lydia (`clear`, Acts 16:14), Selah (`soft`: the Psalms' pause), Nathan (`storyteller`: the prophet who told David a story, 2 Samuel 12), Gideon (`deep`), Caleb (`steady`: who followed wholeheartedly, Numbers 14:24) and Ezra (`wise`: the scribe who taught the Law). No two share a first letter. Never God's, Jesus's, an angel's or a central figure's of the Bible (Moses, David, Mary, Paul), because Scholar never speaks as one; Lydia and not Anna, which sounds like Hannah. The names are the owner's to change.
  2. It stays one Scholar, an AI, and no voice speaks as its name: every voice's opening line is unchanged ("Hi, I’m Scholar, GraceHush’s AI Bible companion. What’s on your heart today?"), the Talk screen's title is still "Scholar" with "Hannah’s voice" under it, and the chat's voice sheet says "Every voice is Scholar, an AI."
